excerpt_original: Why it pays to get lost in the library, what to do if they’re exhuming your great-grandfather and how to make sense of a fragmented reality

blocks.text: Why it pays to get lost in the library, what to do if they’re exhuming your great-grandfather and how to make sense of a fragmented reality

After completing a law degree in the UK, Tan Pin Pin returned to Singapore, postponing her career as a lawyer to pursue her dream of being an artist. With a photography camera in hand, she attended events such as school excursions, funerals and government matchmaking events, documenting everyday scenes, from bus stops to the common areas of government housing. When her career as a filmmaker later took off, these 2,800 or so images ended up being shelved, until recent acquisitions by the Singapore Art Museum required her to dig into her back catalogue.

The newly unearthed images are being shown in a solo exhibition titled Singapore Index as part of the Singapore International Photography Festival, providing a window into life in 1990s Singapore, as well as a glimpse of the dogged chronicler of Singapore life that Tan would later become. What photography and film have in common, she says, is ‘noticing’ – and noticing what has been overlooked or suppressed in the rapid development of the city-state, governed by an efficient but authoritarian political party since its independence, has been her forte.

Over the years, her celebrated documentaries have captured the city’s myriad sights and sounds, its extraordinary urban transformations and the problematic parts of its political history. Singapore GaGa (2005) recorded the city’s soundscapes, which ranged from avant-garde pianist Margaret Leng Tan’s performances to the quirky music of acrobatic street buskers at local subway stations. Invisible City (2007) features interviews with other documentarians, archaeologists and historians, as well as their archival footage.

This was followed by To Singapore, With Love (2013), comprising poignant portraits about an older generation of Singapore’s political exiles who fled the country because of their beliefs and were unable to return for fear of being detained without trial.

Tan’s last full-length documentary, IN TIME TO COME (2017), is more experimental in form – a series of sequences, also filmed in Singapore, stitched together without commentary, including rituals such as flag-raising ceremonies, the pruning of roadside trees and the opening of a new undersea expressway, all of which contain an odd, detached quality.

That sense of the mysterious-mundane also extends to her work in contemporary art contexts, most notably in the 2025 Singapore Biennale , where she showed On a Clear Day You Can See Forever (2025), an installation that juxtaposed 80km/h (2004), a single-take shot out of the window of a taxi driving through Singapore’s Pan-Island Expressway, with footage of Inuka in the Singapore Zoo, the world’s first polar bear born in captivity in the tropics.

On rediscovering the images in Singapore Index , she says: ‘I really wanted to be an artist, and I didn’t dare or know how to be one. Looking at the negatives, I saw that I was proving to myself that I had what it took to be an artist. It makes me think that I didn’t become who I am, I already was [that person].’ In this interview, she shares more about her trajectory of moving from photography to film, filmmaking as a race against time and how, after more than 30 years of creative work set mostly around Singapore, she might move beyond explorations of national identity in her latest film.

blocks.text: Preparing to Jump Ship
ArtReview How did you feel encountering these images in Singapore Index again after so long? Were they a time capsule of a younger Singapore, and a younger Pin Pin?
Tan Pin Pin I don’t feel nostalgic looking at the photos. The subjects still feel very present and there was more life in their faces – people weren’t looking at their phones then!

I had always felt my artistic journey truly began when I made my first film, Moving House , in 1996 [about the exhumation of her great-grandfather’s grave to make way for redevelopment in land-scarce Singapore]. I didn’t think the two photography series, set in Singapore [ Singapore Index , 1991–92] and China [ Another China , 1991], where I also spent some time, were relevant to my oeuvre, but now I feel they are key to my later practice in film. The DNA from these photos are in all my films: using the camera in an exploratory way, on the road alone, bearing witness; curiosity first, then thinking about the images before doing something to them.
AR We often look at old photographs for evidence of what has disappeared. But were there things in this archive that surprised you because they haven’t changed at all?

TPP Actually, if you see the photos, everything apart from the fashion looks contemporary. Someone from China who was in Singapore for the first time told me after she saw the photos, “Singapore existed even then!”
AR You didn’t plan to be an artist, and completed a law degree in the UK. What made you switch tracks?

TPP As a very academically inclined student, I was shuffled along certain channels and thought that certain professions were the only paths in life. But the thing about tertiary education in the UK is that if you go with a totally open mind, random things can catch your eye. I picked up photography through reading books in the library and attending workshops.

When I came back to Singapore, I interned as a photographer at The Straits Times [Singapore’s largest English-language daily] and eventually did become a lawyer for a while. But then I discovered film, which had not been within my worldview because the costs were not feasible. But in 1996, the Sony DCR-VX1000 camera was released, which was ten times better than any other consumer camcorder on the market and really small in size. I bought the camera, jumped ship and never looked back.
How to Be Nosy
AR Tell me more about your first film, Moving House .

TPP I knew that I needed to record the exhumation of my great-grandfather’s tomb for my family’s posterity, and I felt that photography just wasn’t adequate to record the process. It had to be a moving-image work. This film was later used as part of my portfolio to apply for a scholarship to do an MFA [at Northwestern University, in Illinois]. For my graduation thesis, I did Moving House [2001], about the exhumation of a grave of another family, which won the Student Academy Award for Best Documentary. That of course was the more polished film. You could then see the differences in quality before and after an MFA!

AR A lot of your work seems to involve collecting fragments of reality and then discovering relationships between them much later. Do you see yourself as someone who collects things and eventually finds a form for them?

TPP This is a wonderful description of my process. The very hard part isn’t the filming, it is finding the connections between disparate streams of footage I had collected. I spend many months editing my films just to see if such a link exists. Often, a lot of footage is not used because I couldn’t find the link. Oftentimes the edit reveals gaps, so more filming is needed.
AR To what extent is filmmaking intuitive?

TPP When I was an intern at The Straits Times , one of the editors took me out to lunch. We passed by a group of people crouched over something. He said, “A good reporter would go find out what’s happening. You need to develop a nose for it, this wanting to know.” A lot about being a filmmaker is instinctive. It’s about noticing. Everything else is icing on the cake.
AR How do you begin a project? How do you decide if an idea has wings?

TPP If an idea doesn’t let go of me, I feel it is time to examine it further. Usually, my self-initiated, noncommissioned works take many years to complete, so I need to know I am interested in them enough for the long haul.
Where to Put the Polar Bear
AR How important is not knowing what you’re looking for when you begin a project?

TPP I can safely say that I often think I know what I want to do, but in the process of making, new vistas open, so the work ends up being something else. Take Singapore GaGa . At first the idea was to make a CD of sounds of Singapore as a gift for friends going away, or for friends visiting the country for the first time. But since I was collecting sounds, I thought, I might as well bring along a video camera. In the end I made a film out of it.

AR For On a Clear Day You Can See Forever , you juxtaposed 80km/h with footage of Inuka the polar bear swimming in her tank. What made you return to the Inuka footage and place it alongside 80km/h more than two decades after that work was made?

TPP Selene Yap [one of the curators of the 2025 Singapore Biennale] suggested the juxtaposition. She was interested to explore how the two footages were different expressions of time and how they could be in conversation with each other. The form in how the two clips were to be juxtaposed, in the final sculptural format, was decided upon after we looked at the space I had been provided. I wanted the images parallel, not side by side. Inuka was shot in 2006 and also 2010.

blocks.caption: IN TIME TO COME (still), 2017. Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: AR Your films sometimes seem to document things before they become history. Do you have a sense, while filming, that something will one day disappear? Or does that significance only emerge with time?

TPP It depends. I remember distinctively while making both Invisible City and To Singapore, With Love that I had to make these films quickly, as the interviewees were very elderly. However, in IN TIME TO COME I felt that the scenes were enduring, such as flag-raising ceremonies in schools and fire drills; that they would be rituals even 50 years from now.

AR Really? In IN TIME TO COME , everything had a sense of precarity for me. I found the opening sequence of the kayakers in a reservoir in the morning absolutely wonderful. Their energetic shouts, the sounds of the forest, just nature in general.
TPP You thought that it would all be lost 50 years from now? That the water would be all dried up?
An End to Hustling?
AR Exactly. I’m also curious about your own feelings when you look back on your own work. How do you feel revisiting an old series such as Singapore Index , for example?

TPP It’s slightly bittersweet for me to see my juvenilia. When I was young, I was so permanently hustling and on the road. Now, with age, I know I cannot do it; the energy is not there anymore. But my next film is about what it means to be nearly sixty and still making work. It’s a film within a film about Tan Pin Pin making a film, and it’s set in Aliwal Arts Centre, where I have a desk in a coworking space. The film will also feature people with whom I share the building – actors, dancers and so on – and it is also about my wider realisation of the creative world beyond filmmaking.

AR You’ve made films that have been celebrated internationally but also challenged or restricted at home. Has this changed the way you think about your responsibilities as a filmmaker, or your relationship with your audience in Singapore?

TPP I take each work on its own merits. Someone told me that I was brave to follow up To Singapore, With Love , which was political, with IN TIME TO COME , which was experimental. But to me, they both are expressions of my worldview.

blocks.caption: To Singapore, With Love (still), 2013. Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: AR Do you think it’s possible for a documentary filmmaker to remain politically neutral? Or is the very act of choosing what to film and what to leave out already a political decision?
TPP I think choosing to be an artist is already a political act, because it privileges self-expression, which in some countries, including Singapore, is a dangerous thing to strive for.
AR Any upcoming projects?

TPP In December I’ll be part of a group show called Fragments of a Peach Blossom Spring , in which I’ll show five photographs from a series called Views from the Edge [2010], showing views of Singapore from Johor Bahru in Malaysia. I worked on this idea for a few years, driving around in Malaysia wrapping around the Straits of Johor, passing through places such as Pasir Gudang, Stulang Laut and beyond. I was interested in communities living and working with Singapore in their sights. These photos morphed into the film To Singapore, With Love , which grew out of the idea of viewing Singapore from the outside. In fact, the poster for the film is of a man looking over to Singapore on the horizon. I had this image in my mind even before the idea of the film was born.

Fragments of a Peach Blossom Spring will run at Objectifs – Centre for Photography & Film, Singapore, 4–13 December ; Singapore Index is on view at Shop–House by DECK until 31 January as part of the 10th Singapore International Photography Festival; On a Clear Day You Can See Forever will be shown at Rubaiya Qatar 2026, opening in various venues across Doha, 21 November – 30 April
